data.title: Watering Hole and Trusted Third-Party Compromise
data.summary: Staff routinely visited third-party sites specific to their industry and role, which an attacker can compromise to reach this organisation's users without contacting them directly.
data.description:
A watering hole attack inverts phishing: rather than sending something to the target, the attacker compromises a site the target already visits and trusts — an industry body, a supplier portal, a specialist forum, a recruitment site.

Nothing suspicious arrives in the mail, and the victim's behaviour is unchanged, so awareness training offers no protection. Targeting is achieved by choosing a site whose visitors are the intended population.

The same logic applies to third-party script loaded into your own pages: a compromised analytics or payment script executes in your origin, for every visitor, with no compromise of your own systems.
data.recommendation:
* Keep browsers and plugins current, and prefer isolation for high-risk browsing.
* Use Subresource Integrity and a strict Content-Security-Policy for third-party scripts you include, and minimise how many there are.
* Monitor egress for unexpected destinations and for behaviour following a normal web visit.
* Include third-party dependencies in supplier risk assessment, not only the suppliers you contract with directly.
data.short_recommendation: Isolate browsing and verify third-party scripts with SRI.
